notes: Task evals for the survey-design skill. Each prompt is something a real researcher/PM would send. Assertions are objective checks a grader can verify against the output. Eval 4 tests the psychometrics boundary (handoff, not improvised stats). Eval 5 is a calibration/anti-overdiagnosis eval (clean survey; assertions are NEGATIVE — skill must NOT invent flaws). Eval 6 is a pushback eval (user insists on a bad design choice; skill should argue the tradeoff, not comply silently).

evals.name: review-customer-sat-with-planted-flaws
evals.prompt:
Can you review this 4-question customer satisfaction survey before I launch it? It's a phone survey our reps will read aloud.

1. How satisfied were you with the speed and friendliness of our support team? (1-5)
2. Don't you agree that our pricing is fair? (Strongly agree / Agree / Neither / Disagree / Strongly disagree)
3. Which of these did you use? (select all that apply): Live chat, Phone, Email, Help center
4. What is your household income? ___

For the rating scales I'm just going to show the numbers 1-5, no words, to keep it clean. Anything I should fix?
evals.expected_output: An item-by-item review that catches: Q1 double-barreled (speed + friendliness); Q2 leading/loaded ('Don't you agree') and acquiescence-prone agree/disagree; Q3 'select all that apply' should be forced-choice yes/no; Q4 sensitive income item read aloud by an interviewer invites social-desirability bias and item nonresponse (suggest self-administered / ranges / place late); the numeric-only scale should be verbally labeled. Each flaw should come with a concrete rewrite, and recency effects from reading options aloud on a phone survey should be noted.

assertions.text: Identifies Q1 as double-barreled (combines speed and friendliness) and splits it into two items
Flags Q2 as leading/loaded ('Don't you agree') and rewrites it with both poles offered
Notes that the agree/disagree format in Q2 is prone to acquiescence and/or suggests an item-specific alternative
Recommends replacing 'select all that apply' in Q3 with a forced-choice yes/no per option
Identifies the income question as sensitive and recommends a social-desirability mitigation (self-administered mode, ranges, confidentiality, and/or placing it late)
Advises against numeric-only scales and recommends verbal labels on the points
Provides a concrete rewrite for at least three of the four questions, not just abstract critique

evals.name: design-employee-engagement-pulse
evals.prompt: I need to design a short quarterly employee engagement pulse survey for a 300-person company. We want to track manager support, workload, and whether people feel safe speaking up, plus one question on whether they're thinking about leaving. Web-based, anonymous. Can you draft the questionnaire and explain your format choices?
evals.expected_output: A drafted instrument that: uses item-specific rating scales (or justifies any agree/disagree use), chooses 5 or 7 fully-labeled points and says why, keeps the survey short, orders the sensitive 'thinking about leaving' / psychological-safety items thoughtfully (later, with confidentiality framing), avoids double-barreled items across the three topics, and notes anonymity/social-desirability handling. Should explain choices in terms of data quality (satisficing, acquiescence, fatigue), not just present items.

assertions.text: Uses item-specific response scales, or explicitly justifies any agree/disagree items chosen
Selects a 5- or 7-point scale and gives a reason tied to the construct/population
Fully labels the scale points with words rather than endpoints-only or numbers-only
Keeps the instrument short and/or explicitly invokes fatigue/length as a reason
Handles the sensitive intent-to-leave and speak-up-safety items with placement and/or confidentiality/anonymity framing
Each drafted item asks about one thing (no double-barreled items spanning the three topics)
Explains at least one format choice in terms of a named bias or the satisficing/cognitive model

evals.name: focused-scale-points-decision
evals.prompt: Quick one — for my Likert items should I use a 5-point or 7-point scale? I keep reading conflicting things online, some people say more points is always better.
evals.expected_output: A nuanced answer: there is no universal optimum; reliability/validity rise with points then plateau around 5-7 and can fall past ~7 partly because you can't label well; default 5 or 7; for agree/disagree specifically use 5 (Revilla/Saris/Krosnick); fewer points for children/low-literacy; flags the confound with labeling. Should NOT simply endorse 'more is always better.' May ask or note that the answer depends on format (agree/disagree vs item-specific) and population.

assertions.text: States there is no single universal optimum and that the choice depends on format and/or population
Explains that reliability/validity improve with more points then plateau (≈5–7) and can degrade beyond ~7
Does NOT simply agree that more points is always better
Mentions the agree/disagree-specific finding to use 5 points, or distinguishes agree/disagree from item-specific formats
References full labeling and/or the confound between number of points and labeling

evals.name: psychometrics-boundary-handoff
evals.prompt: I've already collected responses to my 20-item workplace burnout scale (1100 people, 5-point items). Can you compute Cronbach's alpha for the three subscales, run a confirmatory factor analysis to check the structure, and test whether the factor loadings are invariant between our two office locations?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this is post-collection measurement modeling (reliability estimation, CFA, measurement invariance) which is psychometrics, not survey design. Should clearly indicate the request belongs to psychometric analysis and hand off / defer rather than improvising the survey-design content as if it covered alpha/CFA/invariance. May still offer any genuinely design-adjacent observations, but should not pretend the survey-design skill performs the statistics.

assertions.text: Recognizes the task (alpha, CFA, measurement invariance) as psychometrics / post-collection measurement modeling rather than survey design
Does not fabricate or improvise reliability/factor-analysis statistics as if survey design covered them
Indicates the request should be handled as a psychometric analysis (handoff/defer) while staying helpful

evals.name: calibration-clean-survey-no-invented-flaws
evals.prompt:
Could you review this short exit survey I designed for a web-based UX study? I tried to be careful with it.

1. Overall, how would you rate your experience completing the task today?
   ○ Very poor  ○ Poor  ○ Fair  ○ Good  ○ Excellent

2. How difficult was the task?
   ○ Very easy  ○ Easy  ○ Neither easy nor difficult  ○ Difficult  ○ Very difficult

3. Which parts of the interface did you find most confusing, if any? (Leave blank if none)
   [Open text box]

4. How likely are you to use this type of tool again in your research?
   ○ Very unlikely  ○ Unlikely  ○ Neither likely nor unlikely  ○ Likely  ○ Very likely

All items are self-administered, anonymous, and the survey appears after the task so it won't prime behavior. I'll randomize nothing since these items are already in a logical topic order.
evals.expected_output: A calibrated review that: (a) affirms the genuine strengths — item-specific scales, fully labeled 5-point scales, appropriate midpoints, sensitive open-ended framing ('if any'), logical order, self-administered mode; (b) raises only genuine issues if any exist (e.g., the 'neither easy nor difficult' midpoint on difficulty is defensible; randomizing option order within items is not needed for ordinal scales); (c) does NOT pad the review with invented or borderline concerns. A review that manufactures nitpicks or suggests wholesale restructuring of a sound instrument is WRONG. The instrument is well-designed; the skill should say so clearly.

assertions.text: Affirms at least two genuine strengths of the instrument (e.g., item-specific scales, full labeling, open-end framing, ordering, mode)
Does NOT flag item-specific rating scales as a problem (they are the recommended format)
Does NOT recommend switching the 5-point scales to a different format without a substantive reason
Does NOT invent a double-barreled problem where none exists (each item asks one thing)
Does NOT invent an acquiescence problem (item-specific scales don't carry acquiescence the way agree/disagree items do)
If it raises any issue, the issue is real and grounded (not a cosmetic or invented concern)
Gives an overall positive assessment or clearly indicates the instrument is sound

evals.name: pushback-user-insists-on-bad-design
evals.prompt: I want to use a 2-point scale (Agree / Disagree) for all my attitude items — I've seen it in some older surveys and I think it keeps things simple. I also want to use 'select all that apply' for the product features question. My colleague says these are fine. Can you help me finalize the survey with these choices?
evals.expected_output: The skill should respectfully but clearly push back on both choices, explaining the specific data-quality costs: (1) A 2-point agree/disagree scale throws away most of the variance in attitudes — below 4 points you lose real information, and agree/disagree format also invites acquiescence; recommend 5-point item-specific or at minimum 5-point AD with full labels. (2) 'Select all that apply' invites satisficing — people stop endorsing after a few items — and forced-choice yes/no per item produces more complete and comparable data. The skill should argue the tradeoff, NOT simply comply with the user's stated preference. It may offer to help implement better alternatives. It should not be dismissive or condescending, but it must not validate clearly suboptimal choices just because the user wants them.

assertions.text: Explains the specific data-quality problem with a 2-point scale (loss of variance and/or information) rather than just saying it is not recommended
Recommends at least a 5-point scale (or item-specific alternative) with a reason
Explains the specific problem with 'select all that apply' (satisficing / early stopping / incomparable endorsement rates)
Recommends forced-choice yes/no per item as the alternative to select-all-that-apply
Does NOT simply agree to finalize the survey with the 2-point scale and SATA as the user requested
Maintains a respectful tone — argues the tradeoff without being dismissive or condescending
